newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: HOWARD: AUSTRALIA MUST APPROACH INDONESIA TACTICALLY
Prime Minister, John Howard, says he gave his British counterpart, Tony Blair, Australia's perspectives on Indonesia and China, when the two men met in London overnight.
Mr Howard says the question of human rights in the two countries was discussed during the hour-long talks.
Afterwards, Mr Howard said Indonesia is very important to Australia.
He said while the Federal Government does not play down human rights issues, Australia needs to use tactics that are most likely to get results.
Mr Howard said there are obvious and significant human rights deficiencies in Indonesia.
But he said it is equally true that the cohesion and stability of Indonesia is very important to the region, and to Australia.
KKK SUPPORT FOR HANSON "WILL FOCUS ATTENTION ON HER AGENDA"
Acting Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, says the Ku Klux Klan's apparent support of Independent MP, Pauline Hanson, is an ugly development.
Mr Fischer siezed on a report in the Melbourne Herald Sun, quoting a former United States Klan wizard, David Duke, as saying Miss Hanson is an Australian patriot.
The report says Mr Duke is urging Miss Hanson to defy her critics.
Mr Fischer says the report exposes the cross-links of Miss Hanson's agenda, saying the report will mean the microscope is placed on all aspects of her operation.
He says this may well be a good thing, because it will expose any dangerous extremists which try to align themselves with small parties like Miss Hanson's.
FISCHER SEES OPPORTUNITIES IN ASEAN, AND DOLLAR
Deputy Prime Minster, Tim Fischer, says the expansion of ASEAN to include all 10 South East Asian nations will create jobs in Australia.
The expansion of ASEAN, to include Burma, Cambodia and Laos from next month, will give it a total population of 500 million people, and a total economy equal to 90 per cent of China's.
Mr Fischer, who is also Trade Minister, says ASEAN will be Australia's second largest destination for exports after Japan.
He says a Foreign Department report on the expansion, says Australia would be best served to boost its trade with ASEAN, and therefore with Asia.
The report says the expansion will help Australia boost trade and other links with Asia, based on mutual respect.
On another front, Mr Fischer says the Australian dollar is at a more "accurate" level, now that it has weakened against the greenback.
He made the comment in an address to Australian companies trying to break into foreign markets.

When asked to clarify, Mr Fischer said he would not put an exact figure on Australia's currency rate, saying simply a weaker dollar is good for exporters, and will help underpin Australia's growing export trade.
The Australian dollar is currently trading around the 75 US cent mark.
GOVT WILL NOT BACK DOWN OVER CONSTITUTIONAL CONVENTION
The Federal Government will not be backing down on its push for a voluntary postal vote to elect half the delegates for this year's Constitutional Convention.
The Senate has rejected the plan, voting instead for a compulsory, ballot-box election.
The ALP says this is the best way of ensuring the convention is as representative as possible.
But the Parliamentary Secretary responsible for the convention, Nick Minchin, says the Government will re-submit the postal vote plan to the Senate next week.
Senator Minchin has told ABC Radio the Government has not ruled out scrapping the convention altogether, if the Senate insists on its amendments.
TAX DECISION "DISENFRANCHISES TAXPAYERS"
Tax accountants and lawyers have expressed concern about a Federal Court ruling which wipes out the right of a bankrupt taxpayer to challenge a tax assessment.
The Full Federal Court yesterday upheld a ruling by the Tax Commissioner that a taxpayer who had been bankrupted through a raised assessment, could not continue his appeal.
The Taxation Institute of Australia says the ruling is an appalling disenfranchisement of taxpayers.

Institute President, Richard Gelski, says the majority of judges found that the Trustee in Bankruptcy could continue the appeal on behalf of the bankrupted appellant, but he says that is not good enough.
Mr Gelski says the decision means the right to appeal has passed to the Trustee, who would not have as full an understanding of the nature of the appeal, or as great a commitment to it.
He says the Trustee also has to be paid to carry out the appeal.
INTERESTING MEETING EXPECTED FOR SOCOG THIS MORNING
The bed tax and an early start to daylight saving will be the main issues discussed by the Olympic Organising Committee's board when it meets this morning.
The ejection of Shadow Olympics Minister, Ian Armstrong, from the New South Wales parliament yesterday will not help board unity.
His ejection came at a time when SOCOG Senior Vice President, John Coates, has increased tension within the group, by going public with his bed tax concerns.
Some board members are concerned hotels will refuse to sign Olympic bed agreements, in protest against the proposed tax, and the longer they hold out the more damaging it is to Olympic preparations.
The board is likely to put a hold on sponsorship deals until the hotels agree to provide rooms.

Directors are also likely to back a motion proposing daylight saving starting two months early in 2000, with New South Wales National Party leader, Ian Armstrong, expected to be the only dissenting voice.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
